opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of the debate around this question has been a little unproductive, because people come in with very different ideas of what "meaning" or "world model" is supposed to refer to. One camp says that a model trained only on text can't, in principle, have access to meaning, because meaning is about the relationship between language and the world, and the model never sees the world. The other camp says that obviously these things understand, look at what they can do. I don't find either of those positions very satisfying.

The way I like to think about it is more operational. Instead of asking "does the model have meaning" as a yes-or-no question, you can ask: are there representations inside the model that behave the way a representation of the world *ought* to behave? If I describe a situation in text, say, a sequence of actions where someone puts a key in a box and then moves the box to another room, does the model build some internal state that tracks where the key is? Can I find that state with a probe? And more importantly, if I intervene on that state, if I edit it so the model "thinks" the key is somewhere else, does its downstream behavior change in the way you'd predict? That last part, the causal intervention, is what I think separates a real model of the situation from a bunch of surface correlations that happen to be decodable.

And when you run experiments like that, the answer you get is kind of interesting and kind of messy. You do find these things. There's real evidence that language models construct representations of entities and their states, of spatial layouts, of the beliefs of characters in a story, that are at least partially structured the way a world model would be. But they're also incomplete and inconsistent in ways that matter. The model might track the state of an object perfectly well in one phrasing and completely lose it in another. It might represent a fact but fail to propagate the consequences of that fact when something changes. So I'd describe what's there as fragments of world models, sort of approximate and patchy, rather than a single coherent simulation of the world.

The other point I'd make is about the in-principle argument. I think it's actually less obvious than people assume that you can't learn anything about meaning from text alone. Text is produced by people who are describing the world, reasoning about it, communicating about it. So the distribution of text carries a huge amount of information about the structure of the world, even if it doesn't carry *all* of it. The real question isn't whether some meaning can be recovered from form, but how much, and which parts. There are probably things, certain perceptual grounding, certain facts about what it's like to act in the world, that are much harder to get from text. But a lot of the relational, inferential, compositional structure of meaning seems to be learnable from the signal.

And practically, I think this framing matters because it gives you something to do with it. If models have these partial, sometimes-wrong world representations, then you can start asking how to make them more coherent: how to find them, how to fix them when they're wrong, how to update them when facts change, how to make sure the model's outputs are actually consistent with what it represents internally. That turns a philosophical argument into a research program, and that's the version of the question I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response proposes operational tests and discusses experimental evidence, but does not state that many mainstream formulations can now be addressed with precise empirical tests.

r002.rationale: It describes the evidence as “kind of interesting and kind of messy,” and characterizes the models’ world representations as incomplete, inconsistent, and patchy rather than giving an unqualified yes or no.

r003.rationale: It identifies evidence for representations of entities and their states, spatial layouts, and characters’ beliefs—structured situation information about entities and their properties or relations.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe copying, local n-gram processing, and world modeling as parallel mechanisms that compete within a model.

r005.rationale: It says a model may track an object’s state under one phrasing but lose it under another, but does not attribute this to a shift in dominance among competing mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "meaning" and what you mean by "world model," and I've spent a lot of time trying to make those terms precise enough that they become empirical questions rather than philosophical ones.

Let me start with where I think the skeptical position is strongest. There's an argument, which Emily Bender and Alexander Koller made really clearly, that if all you ever see is text, you can't learn what the text is about. You see the word "red" next to the word "apple," but you never see an apple. And I think that argument is correct about something, which is that there's a kind of grounding, a connection to referents in the world, that a text-only model just doesn't have in any direct way.

But I think it's wrong about something else, which is what you can learn from text alone. The intuition I'd push on is this: language isn't random. The reason people say the things they say is that they're describing a world, and that world has structure. So the distribution over text is shaped by the distribution over situations that gave rise to it. And if you're a sufficiently powerful learner trying to predict that text, one of the most efficient things you can do is to recover some of that underlying structure.

So the question I actually find productive is: does the model's internal state encode information about the situation the text is describing, and does that representation causally drive what the model does next? That's something you can test. We did some work on this with Othello, where you train a model only on sequences of moves, never show it a board, and then ask whether you can find the board state inside the network. And you can, and more importantly, if you edit that internal representation, the model's predictions change in exactly the way you'd expect if it were really using a board. That's not the full richness of what we mean by a world model, but it's a representation of a world that the model learned purely from descriptions of it.

There's also work from my group with Belinda Li on text-based environments, where you give a model a sequence of instructions and ask what the model believes about the state of the room. And again, you find that the entities and their properties are tracked in the representations, and that those representations are predictive of the model's behavior.

Now, here's the part where I want to be careful. "Has a world model" tends to get read as a binary, and I don't think it is. What we actually find is that these representations are partial, they're sometimes inconsistent, they can be correct in one context and wrong in a context that should be equivalent. A model can represent the board perfectly for the kinds of games it's seen and fall apart on ones it hasn't. So the right picture is something like: there's a representation of the world in there, it's doing real work, and it's also brittle and incomplete in ways that humans' representations typically aren't.

On the meaning question specifically, I'd distinguish two things. One is the kind of meaning that's about internal structure, how words relate to each other and to representations of situations. I think models clearly have that. The other is reference, the connection between a symbol and an actual thing. For a text-only model, that connection is parasitic on us. The word "Paris" in the model points at Paris because it points at Paris for the people who wrote the training data. Whether you want to call that meaning is kind of a terminological choice, but I think it matters practically, because it tells you where to expect failures: anywhere the text was a poor proxy for the world.

So my short version would be: yes, these models build representations of the world, you can find them, you can intervene on them, and they're not just surface statistics. And also, they're not what you'd get from actually interacting with the world, and the interesting research is in characterizing exactly where that gap is rather than arguing about whether it exists.

r001.rationale: The response says the meaning and world-model questions can be made into empirical questions and describes tests that probe internal representations.

r002.rationale: It rejects a binary answer and describes representations as partial, inconsistent, and brittle.

r003.rationale: It reports that models track entities and their properties in text-based environments, and that Othello models encode board states.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe copying, local n-gram processing, and world modeling as parallel competing mechanisms.

r005.rationale: The response does not say that small changes in problem presentation can shift which mechanism dominates.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate a couple of questions that tend to get bundled together. One is whether a language model represents information about the world. Another is whether it represents that information in a way that supports consistent reasoning, prediction, and action. And then there’s the question of whether we want to call any of that understanding.

For the first question, language prediction gives you a reason to learn something about the world, because the world is what people are talking about. If you’re predicting a description of someone moving an object from one place to another, tracking where the object is can help you predict what comes next. So I don’t think the fact that a model is trained to predict text rules out its learning representations of meaning.

But that doesn’t establish that it has a single, coherent world model. It might have representations that work well in some contexts and fail in others. And producing a correct answer doesn’t, by itself, tell us which mechanism it used.

So I’d want to make the question more concrete: What information is represented? When does the model use it? If we change the situation, does its prediction change appropriately? If we intervene on the representation, does that change its behavior in the way we expect? Those questions seem more productive to me than treating ‘has a world model’ as an all-or-nothing property.

r001.rationale: The response proposes concrete empirical questions, but does not state that many mainstream formulations can now be addressed with precise tests.

r002.rationale: It describes representations that may work in some contexts and fail in others, and questions an all-or-nothing framing, conveying conditional rather than categorical answers.

r003.rationale: It gives object tracking as a reason a model might learn world information, but does not identify evidence that models construct structured situation representations of entities and their properties or relations.

r004.rationale: It does not describe copying, local n-gram processing, and world modeling as parallel competing mechanisms.

r005.rationale: It does not state that small changes in problem presentation can shift which competing mechanism dominates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what we mean by a world model. There’s a fairly weak sense in which, to predict language well, you need to know something about the world that produced that language. If you’re predicting a description of somebody moving an object around a room, it helps to keep track of where that object is. And we can ask experimentally whether a model is keeping track of that information and using it to make predictions.

But that’s different from saying that it has a single, coherent model of the world that it consults whenever it answers a question. A model might represent something in one context and fail to use it in another. It might give you answers that suggest an understanding of a situation, but then fail when you change the wording or ask about a consequence of that same situation.

So I’d rather break the question into smaller questions: What information does the model represent? How does it acquire that information? And does that information actually play a causal role in its behavior? You can sometimes decode a fact from a model’s internal representations without showing that the model uses that fact.

I think the same applies to meaning. We can make progress by identifying particular aspects of meaning—reference, relationships between entities, what follows from a sentence—and studying those directly. That seems more productive to me than trying to settle, all at once, whether these systems have meaning or don’t.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers can experimentally test whether models track information, but does not state that many mainstream formulations can now be answered with precise empirical tests.

r002.rationale: It recommends breaking the question into smaller parts and studying particular aspects of meaning, rather than settling the issue with an all-at-once yes or no.

r003.rationale: It gives object location as an example of information a model might track, but does not identify evidence that models construct structured situation representations encoding entities and their properties or relations.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe copying, local n-gram processing, and world modeling as parallel mechanisms that compete.

r005.rationale: It notes that changing wording can affect answers, but does not connect this to changes in which competing mechanism dominates.
